en: Preface to the Newly Carved *Fahua Yanyi* (Explication of the Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra):
In the past, Śākyamuni Tathāgata preached the Dharma for forty-nine years; yet it is only the *Lotus Sūtra* alone that is praised as "pure, perfect, and uniquely wondrous.
This is because, in terms of time, it corresponds to midday, and in terms of flavor, it is the *amṛta* (clarified butter). It was not preached during the first four [periods].
Ten years ago, the time had not yet arrived and the capacity of beings was not yet mature; thus, it was taught only forty years later.

At that point, the provisional could be set aside and the real could be established. By returning the nine realms to the Buddha-realm and unifying the three vehicles into the One Vehicle, the profound, solid, subtle, and far-reaching nature of this sutra becomes incomparable to the "combined," "single," "confrontational," or "interlaced" teachings—how could it be described by mere words and phrases?

How could one possibly fathom it? Nevertheless, the profound significance of the sūtras would not be clarified without explanation, and the central tenets of the sūtras would not be made manifest without propagation.
If one does not employ the common language of the world, how else can one assist in proclaiming the Buddha-dharma?
Therefore, since the Chen and Sui dynasties, there have been many commentators, yet none has rivaled Tiantai in his analytical exposition.
Nanyue said to Tiantai: "Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, none but you can realize it, and none but I can recognize it.
Even if there were a thousand or ten thousand teachers of letters, none could exhaust your analytical eloquence. This was Nanyue.
Tiantai certainly listened to the *Lotus Sūtra* together with him; he came directly from Mount Ling. Subsequently, Jingxi of the Tang dynasty merely produced the *Shiqian*;
Wenzheng of the Song dynasty had only the *Yaoyi*; and as for the Yuan dynasty, there was the printed edition of the *Kezhu*.
Without imposing my own views, I have instead composed these annotations based on the established teachings of Tiantai.
From the Ming Dynasty down to the present dynasty, there have appeared further works such as the *Huìyì* (Compendium of Meanings) and the *Shòushǒuzhǐzhǎng* (Pointing to the Fingers and Palms).

Although it is said that "only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively fathom [the truth]," those who are able to clarify the meaning of the scriptures and manifest their essential purport are all emissaries of the Tathāgata. — Xiu Rou of Dong’ou.
The Dharma Master has spent many years immersed in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Having expounded the sutra on five occasions, his lecture halls have flourished.

Now, taking the draft of Master Yisong, he has categorized the sections and arranged the paragraphs, correcting errors and supplementing omissions. Where the scriptural commentary and the meaning coincide, the text has been restored to its perfection.
Desiring now to publish this among the woodblocks, he sought my consultation. I read and recited it, observing how it elucidates [the text].
The meaning of the sutras is clearly distinguished and made lucid, as bright as the sun at midday.

It expounds the essential purport of the scriptures with such purity and refinement that it possesses the rich flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter). The pearls are linked and the veins are threaded together; the dross is removed while the essence remains.
He abridged what previous sages had detailed and elaborated upon what they had omitted. He presented the profound through the simple and manifested the obscure through the clear.
Adapting to the needs of the times and serving as the very essence of goodness, how could he be considered inferior to the ancient masters?
Generally speaking, there are certain underlying principles governing the transmission of scriptures and texts; it was by these that the pine tree of that day [was preserved].
The original manuscript of this work was not placed into the hands of Dharma Master Xiaorou; had it not been so, this manuscript would surely have perished and failed to be transmitted.
Even if it had been kept within a casket, had there not been the karmic conditions for its examination within the Tripiṭaka, it likely would not have been edited and collated;
thus, this manuscript too would have remained incomplete and unfinished. Viewed from this perspective, Dharma Master Xiaorou was truly a...
He was the reincarnation of Great Master Matsuo. "If there is no one before, though something be beautiful, it will not be manifested;

if there is no one after, though something be flourishing, it will not be transmitted. Is this not what is meant by this? These two masters, succeeding one another in turn, together brought their work to fulfillment.
How could such a person not be a messenger dispatched by the Tathāgata? The "Chapter on the Dharma Master" states:

"After my parinirvāṇa, if one can secretly preach even a single verse of the Lotus Sūtra for the sake of a single person, you should know that this person is a messenger of the Tathāgata, sent by the Tathāgata, and performing the work of the Tathāgata;
how much more so if they extensively expound this sūtra and explain its meaning. Thus it is said for those who study later.
Whoever obtains this scripture and reads it will fully know the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and will naturally be able to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
How, then, could they worry about not attaining the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
Thus, the merit of the two masters’ gift of the Dharma is truly ineffable. That it is ineffable is by no means my own private word alone. (Guxu Wuyin)
In the third month of summer in the Year of the Tiger, the layman Wu Zhengheng respectfully writes this preface for the newly carved edition of the *Fahua yanyi*.
As for the *Fahua yanyi*, it is the lecture record of Master Yisong. It is unknown where the Master was from.
The era of this [text] has likewise not been clarified; let it be set aside for the time being without further investigation.

I have heard that for a Bodhisattva, the arousal of the mind and the making of vows come first, while attaining the realization of the Way takes non-mindfulness as its foundation (these six characters were seen within a dream). When the mind is empty, the essential meaning is penetrated; when the vow is established, the Path is perfected.

Thereafter, when discussing emptiness, the intent does not reside in emptiness; when speaking of the existence of the mind, the mind is fundamentally non-existent. That the mind is fundamentally non-existent means that existence is wondrous existence (*prajñā-sat*).
When the intent does not reside in emptiness, emptiness is true emptiness (*bhūta-śūnyatā*); true emptiness is not empty. Thus flourishes the contemplative teaching of all Buddhas.

That wondrous existence is not existence causes the deluded views of sentient beings to be transformed. This is a warning for those of ordinary kind who are mired in confusion throughout the four modes of birth.
He does not pass away; this is the realization attained within the Buddha-family, wherein the two deaths are forever extinguished.

Thus we know that although the Tathāgata manifested birth during the Zhou dynasty and again entered *nirvāṇa*, in reality he has long since attained perfect enlightenment and dwells eternally in the world.

Therefore, the "Life Span of the Tathāgata" chapter of this sutra says: "Since I attained Buddhahood, it has been exceedingly long ago; my lifespan is immeasurable, for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas."
The eternally abiding and indestructible lifespan that I originally attained while practicing the bodhisattva path is still not yet exhausted today.
The *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Chapter Sixty-three, "On Past Deeds," states:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, "In the past, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), inconceivable, beginningless worlds, and unspeakable eons ago, there appeared a Tathāgata named Indradhvaja."
“World-Honored One, do you know who he is? The bhikṣus remained silent and gave no answer.

At that time, Mañjuśrī came from the east, from the land called Moonlight Adornment, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Indradhvaja of former times is none other than the World-Honored One now.
Why is this? It is because the World-Honored One is fully endowed with inconceivable and skillful means.”
He brings sentient beings to maturity. In past ages, he has already manifested as eight hundred million Buddhas, yet he had no intention of grasping at perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, in future ages, he will manifest as immeasurable Buddhas. How great is the inconceivable divine transformation of the Tathāgata!
It is like events in a dream—neither past nor present; it is like an image in a mirror—neither real nor false. Like...
The moon in the water is neither existent nor non-existent. Like a person in a painting, it neither comes nor goes; it is neither ancient nor modern.
To seal mind with mind, mind after mind is no different. It is neither real nor empty. When rolled up, there is no length; when unfurled, it is immeasurable.

Neither existent nor non-existent, taking it does not constitute attainment, and letting go does not constitute separation. Neither coming nor going, the Buddha-body is eternally abiding. At the beginning...
It never migrates. Therefore, all sentient beings, from the beginningless past through the endless future, eternally abide within the Buddha-body, never having moved or changed.
Thus, when Bodhisattvas practice self-benefit and the benefit of others for a long duration, both ultimately converge into one.
Through accumulating eons of benefiting others and oneself, the distinction between self and other is ultimately forgotten. Should there be even a single...
If even a hair’s breadth of dharma were not the Way, it would immediately become an obstruction, and the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of the *Lotus Sūtra* could not be perfected.
For this reason, the Tathāgata appeared in the world for the sake of the one great causal event (*ekamahākaruṇā-kāraṇa*), in order to fulfill his original intention.
From the "milk" stage to the final "clarified butter" (*sarpis*), although each was appropriate to its time, he never yet spoke of the true reality of all dharmas.
Because their spiritual capacities were not yet mature, the Buddha’s teaching was not yet perfected. Although the flavor of milk is sudden, it still involves dualistic exposition.

That which is elucidated in the Tripiṭaka is entirely subject to arising and ceasing; even the Vaipulya sūtras still involve refutation and censure, and their matured flavor still carries elements of refinement and elimination.

Even though the Nirvāṇa Sūtra shares the same flavor, it further speaks of the subsequent submergence [of all distinctions]. Therefore, only this sūtra is purely perfect and uniquely sublime. If there is...
Those who hear this Dharma shall not fail to attain Buddhahood; the nine realms will all find their way home, and the three vehicles will all converge.

From this point on, the Great Matter of the Tathāgata’s purpose will be clarified, and his original intent for appearing in the world will be fully realized. Therefore, it is called the "Wondrous Dharma."

Because the Dharma is wondrous, its purport is neither identical nor different. Thus, after Master Tiantai realized samādhi on Mount Dasu, he grasped its main principles and pulled its collar to propagate this wondrous sutra, expanding it into the Three Great Works. This is precisely how they become increasingly identical yet increasingly different.
Subsequent works, such as the *Shiqian*, the *Miaole*, and even this present text, ultimately return to the wondrous [teachings] of the Royal City (the *Lotus Sūtra*).
The essential point is this: it is that the more they differ, the more they coincide. Such is its meaning; layer upon layer of inclusion truly transcends the inconceivable.
Nevertheless, the draft of these lecture records was originally preserved at Jiguang Temple in Dong’ou during the eighth year of the Xianfeng era.
When the Elder Yujian passed away, all his scriptures were scattered and lost, leaving only this draft behind. Although...
I have obtained the complete text. It is entirely worn out and decayed. There is no original manuscript within it, and the *ke* (commentary/sectioning) has not been separately issued.

Alas, when the late master’s disciple Lingshu instructed the layman Kang Sheng to transcribe it, many characters were lost or corrupted. Nevertheless, I cherish it as if it were a divine pearl, protecting it with the value of a moment’s jewel.
I constantly wear it upon my person, never parting from it even while traveling among the clouds and waters, until the time of my final testament. I leave this as my bequest.
How brilliant! Thus, even in the intervals between sleeping and eating, he did not abandon this love [for the Dharma].

In the summer of the *bingzi* year of the Guangxu era, while residing at Chuan Deng Temple in Gu Yue to read the Tripitaka, he obtained a single volume titled *Fahua Shoushou*, which had been selected for inclusion by our present dynasty.
For this reason, I have come to think that Master Song’s lecture notes may well rival [the original work] in excellence.

Should these be lost to posterity, it would not only betray Master Song’s lifelong vows and his heart of blood-drops, but would also fail the many worthies who have long awaited a guiding manual and remain ignorant of where to turn for refuge.
Yet, regarding these drafts, I find myself unable to begin, and yet I cannot let them go—reaching thus far into the third month of midwinter.

On this day, I bathed and burned incense, making a vow as I took up my brush. I kept these thoughts in mind at every moment until the twelfth day, when my reflections were exhausted and my deliberations ceased.
That night, I dreamed of white light illuminating everything everywhere; it was as if a voice said, "Attaining the meaning has 'no-mind' (wúxīn) as its foundation.

These six characters appeared clearly and distinctly before me. Upon waking, I suddenly felt a sense of exhilaration and clarity; joy and a sense of transgression mingled within my breast. Alas! Truly, for myself—

How shameful! I possess no pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) at all, yet I dare to hope for a sacred response. This is truly because [the Buddha], out of compassion for my inferior intelligence, saw that this great task was difficult to accomplish;
thus, he bestowed his grace upon me from the hidden realm, and only then could I fulfill the end. These are indeed straightforward words and not false speech.

Therefore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-sūtra* states: "In the world above, the Tranquil and Peaceful World, the Tathāgata Subtle Cognition, according to the faculties of sentient beings, employs expedient means..."
He manifested the auspicious posture of sleep, and the multitude emulated him; thus, within their dreams, his spiritual consciousness preached the Dharma.
All who were transformed and attained awakening, even those who reached the realization of the Way, had their Buddha-activities performed within their dreams. Now (I, He), am likewise the same.
Relying upon these causes and conditions, I shall take this draft, deleting what is redundant, correcting what is erroneous, and restoring what has been lost.

I have supplemented what was missing and completed what was incomplete. Furthermore, I have organized the sequence of the sections and arranged them in order, inserting the main text and placing the lecture notes beneath it for clarification.
This ensures that readers may understand the material as clearly as seeing their own eyebrows. Because the main text is now present, the work can no longer be called "Lecture Notes" (*jianglu*);
therefore, I have changed the title to *Yanyi* (Exposition of Meaning). It is now entrusted to the carvers to be widely circulated for the sake of future generations.

Fellow students, upon seeing or hearing this, do not become mired in the literal words. Let the vital energy of the mind give rise to understanding so that each may attain the opening, showing, awakening, and entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Realize that what all Buddhas have realized is inherently possessed by all sentient beings.

For those who have not yet resolved to attain Bodhicitta, cause them to resolve quickly; for those who have already resolved to attain Bodhicitta, cause them never to regress from supreme enlightenment.

For those who have already attained non-retrogression, may they swiftly fulfill their vows through an unceasing succession of generations. From this point forward, the Buddha-sun shall increase in brilliance;

it shall be revered from generation to generation, and the Wheel of Dharma shall turn perpetually. Originating from Vulture Peak and extending to the Dragon Flower Assembly, I have thus set forth the account of its origins.
On an auspicious day in the second month of winter in the year of Bingzi, the second year of the Guangxu era of the Great Qing, Xiaorou,
a Buddhist disciple of Manlian from Dong’ou, reverently composed this preface at the Tripitaka Library of Chuan Deng Temple in Gu Yue.
